title: Two-means as a measuring instrument
subtitle: Exactly three Lloyd iterations, seeded at the first and last member, as the fixed definition behind clustering tendency, fragmentation, sub-cluster count and silhouette

stats.label: cluster metrics read from one fixed split
members per second, about half a million, linear in size
or less for the silhouette on the clusters it meets

lede: Does this cluster want to be two clusters? The usual answer is to run k-means with k equal to two and look at the result, and the usual problem is that k-means is an optimiser: it runs until it converges, converges somewhere different depending on its seeds, and gives a different answer on a different day. I wanted the answer to be a metric, which means a fixed procedure with a fixed result. So the two-means split in my engine is defined as a measuring instrument, and four metrics read from it. One block per cluster. A first pass computes the single-centroid inertia, the sum of squared distances to the cluster's own centroid.
quote: A converged k-means gives a better split and a worse metric.
evidence: Deterministic GPU computation: a fixed two-means procedure, first and last member as seeds and exactly three Lloyd iterations, so a cluster splits the same way on the GPU and in the CPU reference.
CUDA kernel development: one block per cluster with no atomics and about 12 KB of shared memory, at about 0.5M members a second, linear in size.
Embedding analytics and cluster metrics: four metrics read from one split, tendency, fragmentation, sub-cluster count and silhouette, the silhouette in 1.2 ms or less for the clusters it meets.
Measurement design: a fixed instrument chosen over a converged optimiser, because a decision rule needs a number that is comparable across a corpus and across runs.
author: Corey James
